questions.knowledge_point: Solving a Second-Order ODE When the Right-Hand Side and the Complementary Solution are Dependent
questions.problem:
Find the general solution to the problem

$$
{y}^{″}+y=8\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x),$ which is the solution to the homogeneous equation

$$
{y}^{″}+y=0.
$$

Writing down and solving the auxiliary equation gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+1 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

So $\lambda =\pm \text{i}$, and therefore the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{c}=P\operatorname{cos}⁡x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

We now need to find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x).$

The particular solution of the inhomogeneous equation cannot be of the form $\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡x$ because this is already included in the complementary function. Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form
y_p = x (\alpha \cos x + \beta \sin x),
]
where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & =(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡x)+x(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\ {y}_{p}^{″} & =2(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡x)+x(-\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡x-\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation:

$$
2(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡x)+x(-\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡x-\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡x)+x(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡x)=8\operatorname{sin}⁡x
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives

$$
-2\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡x+2\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡x=8\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}2\beta =0\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\ -2\alpha =8\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-4$ and $\beta =0.$

Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=-4x\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

The general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

and therefore, the general solution in our case is

$$
y={y}_{c}+{y}_{p}=P\operatorname{cos}⁡x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡x-4x\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x),$ which is the solution to the homogeneous equation

$$
{y}^{″}-{y}^{′}-2y=0.
$$

Writing down and solving the auxiliary equation gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-\lambda -2 & =0 \\ (\lambda +1)(\lambda -2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So $\lambda =-1$ or $\lambda =2$, and therefore the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{-x}+B{e}^{2x}.
$$

We now need to find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x).$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $3\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x.$ Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡x,
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {y}^{″} & =-\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡x-\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation:

$$
-\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡x-\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡x-(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡x)-2(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡x)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives:

$$
(-3\alpha -\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡x+(\alpha -3\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}-3\alpha -\beta =3\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\ \alpha -3\beta =-1\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-1,$ $\beta =0.$

Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

The general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

and therefore, the general solution in our case is

$$
y=A{e}^{-x}+B{e}^{2x}-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

Now let us find constants $A$ and $B.$ 

Substituting $y(0)=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
A+B-1=0.
$$

We now need to apply the condition ${y}^{′}(0)=-1.$ First, we differentiate $y$ to find ${y}^{′}$:

$$
{y}^{′}=-A{e}^{-x}+2B{e}^{2x}+\operatorname{sin}⁡x
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(0)=-1$ into the above gives

$$
-A+2B=-1.
$$

Therefore, we have the following system of equations for $A$ and $B$:

$$
{\begin{aligned}A+B=1 \\ -A+2B=-1\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $A=1,$ $B=0.$
Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y={e}^{-x}-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

questions.problem:
Given that the differential equation 

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-4y=8\operatorname{cos}⁡2x
$$

has the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{-2x}+B{e}^{2x},$ find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ to this equation.
questions.worked_solution:
The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $8\operatorname{cos}⁡2x.$ So we assume the particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡2x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡2x.
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x} & =-2\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡2x+2\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡2x \\ \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =-4\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡2x-4\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡2x.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation:

$$
(-4\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡2x-4\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡2x)-4(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡2x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡2x)=8\operatorname{cos}⁡2x
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives

$$
-8\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡2x-8\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡2x=8\operatorname{cos}⁡2x.
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}-8\alpha =8\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡2x) \\ -8\beta =0\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡2x)\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-1,$ $\beta =0.$

Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=-\operatorname{cos}⁡2x.
$$

questions.problem:
Given that the differential equation 

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+36y=-12\operatorname{cos}⁡6x
$$

has the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)=A\operatorname{cos}⁡6x+B\operatorname{sin}⁡6x,$ find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ to this equation.
questions.worked_solution:
The particular solution of the inhomogeneous equation cannot be of the form $\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡6x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡6x$ because this is already included in the complementary function. Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=x(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡6x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡6x),
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x} & =(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡6x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡6x)+6x(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡6x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡6x) \\ \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =12(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡6x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡6x)-36x(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡6x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡6x)\end{aligned}
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation:

$$
12(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡6x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡6x)-36x(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡6x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡6x)+36x(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡6x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡6x)=-12\operatorname{cos}⁡6x
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives

$$
-12\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡6x+12\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡6x=-12\operatorname{cos}⁡6x.
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}12\beta =-12\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡6x) \\ -12\alpha =0\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡6x)\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =0$ and $\beta =-1.$ Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=-x\operatorname{sin}⁡6x.
$$

questions.problem:
Given that the differential equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-3\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2y=20\operatorname{cos}⁡2x
$$

has the general solution

$$
y(x)=A{e}^{x}+B{e}^{2x}-3\operatorname{sin}⁡2x-\operatorname{cos}⁡2x,
$$

solve the initial value problem

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-3\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2y=20\operatorname{cos}⁡2x,\,y(0)=3,\,{y}^{′}(0)=0.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We find the constants $A$ and $B$ by substituting the initial conditions.

- Substituting $y(0)=3$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}3 & =A{e}^{0}+B{e}^{2(0)}-3\operatorname{sin}⁡2(0)-\operatorname{cos}⁡2(0) \\ 3 & =A+B-1 \\ 4 & =A+B.\end{aligned}
$$

- Differentiating $y$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=A{e}^{x}+2B{e}^{2x}-6\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+2\operatorname{sin}⁡2x.
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(0)=0$ into the derivative gives

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =A{e}^{0}+2B{e}^{2(0)}-6\operatorname{cos}⁡2(0)+2\operatorname{sin}⁡2(0) \\ 0 & =A+2B-6 \\ 6 & =A+2B.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following system of equations for $A$ and $B:$

$$
{\begin{aligned}A+B=4 \\ A+2B=6\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $A=2,B=2.$

Finally, since $A=2$ and $B=2,$ we have the following solution to the initial value problem:

$$
y=2{e}^{x}+2{e}^{2x}-3\operatorname{sin}⁡2x-\operatorname{cos}⁡2x
$$
